Name: reasoning_scaffold_collapse
Title: When Reasoning Becomes a Vestige: Tracing the Formation of an Internalized-Answer Circuit Across RL Training
Short Hypothesis: As a reasoning model is fine-tuned, its verbal chain-of-thought progressively decouples from the computation that actually produces the answer: an 'internalized-answer' representation forms and sharpens across checkpoints, committing to the correct answer earlier and earlier (in fewer reasoning tokens) even as the visible CoT stays long. Overthinking is the residual verbal scaffold left behind after this internal circuit has already formed. This decoupling is measurable checkpoint-by-checkpoint, its onset predicts when a CoT can be safely shortened, and it can be located as a latent-answer direction whose emergence is traceable to the training stage.
Related Work: Prior work observes, behaviorally, that reasoning tokens expand-peak-contract during fine-tuning (Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning 2025), that an optimal CoT length shrinks as capability grows (When More is Less 2025; CoT-Space 2025), that RL compresses exploratory paths and optimizes a sparse subset of tokens (Towards a Mechanistic Understanding survey 2026; Reshaping Reasoning 2025), and that base models already contain reasoning mechanisms that post-training merely learns to deploy at the right time (Base Models Know How, Thinking Models Learn When 2025; AdaptThink, AutoThink, SAGE, JET 2025). All of these are either purely behavioral (token-count curves, accuracy-length tradeoffs) or intervene with RL objectives to shorten CoT. None traces, at the representational level and across training checkpoints, WHEN and HOW an internalized-answer signal forms that makes the verbal CoT redundant. Our contribution is a Formation-Tracing + Location account: we treat the latent answer-commitment as an internal component, measure the checkpoint at which it emerges and how early-in-CoT it fires, and show overthinking is the widening gap between an increasingly-early internal commitment and a slowly-shrinking verbal trace. This reframes existing behavioral observations as the surface signature of a locatable, forming internal circuit, and is distinct from all my prior single-checkpoint proposals (which read signals in one fixed model).
Abstract: Reasoning language models produce long chains of thought, and it is widely observed that reasoning length expands then contracts during fine-tuning while accuracy keeps rising. We ask a mechanistic, training-time question that the behavioral literature leaves open: as training proceeds, does an internal answer-commitment signal form that makes the visible chain of thought increasingly vestigial? We hypothesize that fine-tuning grows and sharpens an internalized-answer representation which commits to the correct answer earlier and earlier within the reasoning trace, so that overthinking becomes the residual verbal scaffold left after this internal circuit has already fired. Using publicly available intermediate checkpoints of open reasoning training runs (e.g., open-source R1-style RL/SFT runs on Qwen/Llama backbones) and, where checkpoints are unavailable, a controlled in-lab GRPO/SFT fine-tune of a small backbone, we trace across checkpoints (1) the step at which a linear latent-answer probe first correctly predicts the final answer within each trace (the internal commitment point), and (2) the length of the verbal trace. On GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA we test whether the commitment point moves earlier across training faster than the verbal trace shrinks, opening a growing commitment-to-trace gap that quantifies vestigial reasoning. We localize the latent-answer direction, validate it causally via truncate-at-commitment and activation patching, and track when this direction emerges over training. Finally we show the per-checkpoint commitment point yields a training-free, checkpoint-aware early-exit that shortens CoT with minimal accuracy loss. Our work reframes overthinking as the surface residue of a forming internalized-answer circuit and gives it a traceable developmental account.
Experiments:
Checkpoint source (shared by all experiments): the study needs a training trajectory, so we use two sources. Primary: publicly released intermediate checkpoints of an open R1-style SFT+GRPO run on a small backbone (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B) if a run with >= 6 saved steps is available. Fallback, always run for control: an in-lab fine-tune of Qwen2.5-1.5B-base (and 7B-base if budget allows) with SFT-then-GRPO on math, saving 8 checkpoints at even intervals from base to converged - this fits an academic budget on one 80GB GPU over a few days for 1.5B. Backbone weights are frozen at inference; only linear probes are trained. Evaluation traces use temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 3 samples per problem with seeds {0,1,2}. Datasets are existing sets: GSM8K test (1319; sample 400), MATH500 (500; all), AIME 2024+2025 (60; all), GPQA-Diamond (198; all), stratified so answers are extractable.

Experiment 1 (H4 - a latent-answer direction exists and can be read within a trace): Tests whether a linear probe / logit-lens can decode the model's eventual final answer from mid-trace activations. Data: for the converged checkpoint first, segment each CoT into reasoning steps and, at each step boundary, record residual-stream activations at the last position; label = the trace's eventual final answer token(s). Train a linear (logistic/ridge) probe on 70% of problems, validate/test on 15/15 split by problem. Compare probe decoding against training-free logit-lens decoding at the same positions. Systems compared: linear probe vs logit-lens vs a majority-answer baseline. Decisive metric: held-out step-level accuracy of predicting the eventual answer as a function of trace position, first; specifically the fraction of traces for which the decoded answer becomes correct-and-stable before the trace ends. Convincing: probe reaches >= 80% eventual-answer accuracy by the final third of the trace on held-out problems and logit-lens corroborates the same commitment ordering (rank correlation >= 0.5). Indecision band: 60-80% final-third accuracy is a usable-but-weak read reported with caution. Negative result: < 60% means no reliable latent-answer signal, blocking the commitment-point construction and undercutting H4.

Experiment 2 (H1 - the internal commitment point moves earlier across training): Tests whether, checkpoint by checkpoint, the model commits to its answer earlier within the trace. Data: apply the Experiment-1 probe/logit-lens (a fresh probe trained per checkpoint on held-out data, with matched probe capacity to avoid capacity confounds) to all four datasets at every checkpoint. Define the COMMITMENT POINT = earliest step after which the decoded answer matches the final answer and stays stable for k=2 steps, expressed as a fraction of trace length. Systems compared: commitment point across the ordered checkpoints; probe-based vs probe-free (logit-lens) commitment as corroboration. Decisive metric: trend of mean commitment-point fraction across checkpoints, first (accuracy and probe AUROC reported alongside so a moving probe cannot masquerade as a moving commitment). Convincing: commitment fraction decreases monotonically across the second half of training by >= 0.15 (e.g., from ~0.7 to <=0.55 of the trace), consistent between probe and logit-lens, while per-checkpoint accuracy is non-decreasing. Indecision band: a decrease of 0.05-0.15, or probe/logit-lens disagreeing on direction, does not decide H1. Negative result: no earlier movement (or movement explained by rising probe accuracy alone) refutes the sharpening-commitment claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 - overthinking is vestigial scaffold: the commitment-to-trace gap grows and post-commitment tokens are redundant): Tests whether tokens generated after commitment grow across training and are causally unnecessary. Data: reuses Experiment 2 measurements plus a causal test. Part A (gap trajectory): per checkpoint record (i) commitment fraction, (ii) mean verbal trace length, (iii) accuracy, and compute the commitment-to-trace GAP = tokens generated after the commitment point; plot against the behavioral expand-peak-contract length curve to show the gap is invisible from length alone. Part B (causal redundancy): on a 150-problem subsample per checkpoint, truncate generation at the decoded commitment point and force the answer, versus truncating at matched random earlier and later steps; measure accuracy retention. Systems compared: truncate-at-commitment vs truncate-earlier vs truncate-later vs full trace. Decisive metric: accuracy retained when truncating at commitment relative to full trace, first; plus the gap trajectory across checkpoints. Convincing: truncating at commitment retains accuracy within 2 points of the full trace while truncating one step earlier costs >= 5 points, AND the gap grows across the second half of training. Indecision band: a 2-5 point accuracy loss at commitment, or a flat gap trajectory, gives only partial support - post-commitment tokens are then not clearly vestigial. Negative result: truncating at commitment costing > 5 points means post-commitment reasoning is genuinely used (useful late verification), refuting the vestigial-scaffold framing of H2.

Experiment 4 (H4 - the latent-answer direction is causally load-bearing and its emergence is traceable to training stage): Tests whether the direction causally drives answering and when it forms. Data: converged and mid checkpoints; frozen backbone. Part A (causal location): localize the latent-answer direction via difference-of-means (committed vs uncommitted step states) and probe weights; patch the committed-answer representation from a late position into an earlier position and test whether it induces early answer commitment; control with a matched-random-direction patch of equal norm. Part B (formation tracing): track probe decoding accuracy for the direction and the principal-angle stability of the direction across all checkpoints, including the base model before fine-tuning, to test whether it is already weakly present in the base model and sharpens with training. Systems compared: real patch vs random-direction patch; direction at base vs early vs late checkpoints. Decisive metric: fraction of trials where injecting the late committed representation induces the correct early answer (vs random-direction control), first; plus the checkpoint at which probe accuracy for the direction first exceeds the Experiment-1 threshold. Convincing: real patch induces early commitment in >= 50% of trials vs < 15% for the random control, and the direction's decodability rises across checkpoints (base weakly decodable, late sharply), with principal angle showing a stabilizing direction. Indecision band: a 20-50% patch effect, or a non-monotone emergence, is partial support. Negative result: patch effect < 20% or indistinguishable from the base model means the direction is not causally load-bearing or not training-formed, refuting H4.

Experiment 5 (H3 - the commitment point yields a checkpoint-aware early-exit): Tests whether stopping at the traced commitment point shortens CoT with minimal accuracy loss. Data: full GSM8K sample (400), MATH500 (500), AIME (60), GPQA (198) on the converged checkpoint (and one mid checkpoint to test that the safe exit tracks the traced commitment). Early-exit rule: stop when the probe is stable and confident for k steps. Systems compared: commitment-based early-exit vs a reactive confidence-exit baseline vs fixed-fraction truncation vs full trace. Decisive metric: token reduction at matched accuracy (accuracy within 1 point of full trace), first; plus whether the empirically safe exit point coincides with the traced commitment point. Convincing: commitment-based exit cuts mean thinking tokens by >= 20% within 1 point of full-trace accuracy and beats fixed-fraction truncation at matched accuracy; and the safe exit shifts earlier at later checkpoints as Experiment 2 predicts. Indecision band: a 5-20% reduction, or parity with (not beating) the reactive baseline, is a marginal result. Negative result: < 5% reduction or > 2 point accuracy loss means the traced commitment point is not actionable for early exit, refuting H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Publicly released intermediate reasoning checkpoints may be scarce or coarse; the in-lab controlled fine-tune fallback keeps the study feasible but limits scale to small backbones, so training-stage claims may not transfer to frontier models (an acknowledged boundary). The latent-answer probe is reliable mainly for extractable answers, restricting to math/multiple-choice. Probe accuracy itself changes across checkpoints, which could confound the commitment-point measurement; we control by using held-out validation, matched probe capacity per checkpoint, and reporting logit-lens (probe-free) commitment as a corroborating measure. The commitment-to-trace gap could reflect genuinely useful late verification rather than vestigial scaffold; the truncate-at-commitment causal test and hard-strata accuracy analysis address whether post-commitment tokens are actually redundant (a null here is itself informative). Activation patching across a forming circuit may be noisy at early checkpoints. Early-exit gains may not exceed strong reactive baselines, but the developmental/formation account of overthinking is the primary standalone contribution. Results may be training-recipe and model-family specific.
